chunks.text: In short

Four loyalty models compete for an independent operator’s setup time: paper punch cards, integrated P O S loyalty (Toast/Square), standalone platforms (Fivestars/Como), and CRM-direct (Mailchimp/Klaviyo + own checkout).
Paper punch cards return 75:1 on a 500-customer base; standalone platforms return 1.17:1; CRM-direct returns ~7x the punch card but only when the direct channel is already converting.
The loyalty conversation is downstream of the channel conversation — fix the channel first, layer the loyalty after, on the direct surface where margin can fund a real customer relationship.
Op-ed · May 11, twenty twenty-six · 7 min read · By Don Goldstein

Four loyalty models compete for the independent restaurant operator’s setup time and monthly fee. Three of them don’t pay back. One does, but only when the kitchen is already running a healthy direct channel. Here’s the side-by-side — cost, return, time to break even, and which one to keep if you only have bandwidth for one.

I ran two of these programs for over a year on the same restaurant, then dropped both and replaced them with a third. The numbers below are mine, not industry benchmarks. Your conversion rates and average check will differ. The order of magnitude is what carries the argument: the gap between the best and worst model isn’t 20%, it’s 4x.
The four models in play.

Every loyalty program a US independent restaurant runs in twenty twenty-six fits one of four shapes. The implementations differ; the underlying economics don’t. Walk through them in order of operator cost-to-implement.

Four loyalty program models for independent restaurants, compared on monthly cost, twelve-month return, and break-even threshold. Model one: paper punch cards. Monthly cost is essentially zero, ten dollars in printing. Twelve-month return on a five-hundred-customer base is about seven hundred fifty dollars in repeat-visit margin. Break-even is under a month. The hard truth: punch cards work but are inherently capped at low frequency and have no operator-side analytics. Model two: integrated P O S loyalty like Toast Rewards or Square Loyalty. Monthly cost is forty-five to seventy-five dollars depending on terminal count. Twelve-month return on the same base is approximately two thousand four hundred dollars, three point two times the punch card. Break-even is roughly four months in. The catch: the P O S controls the data, so when you change processors, the loyalty data does not come with you. Model three: standalone loyalty platforms like Fivestars or Como Sense. Monthly cost is one hundred sixty-five to two hundred forty-nine dollars. Twelve-month return is about two thousand eight hundred dollars, slightly better than the integrated P O S but only because the platforms invest more in SMS reactivation. Break-even is around month seven. The catch: the SMS reactivation campaigns can feel spammy and you lose customers to opt-outs at a faster rate than the program acquires them past month nine. Model four: a CRM stitched to your own checkout, run through Mailchimp or Klaviyo with a customer-segment loyalty layer on the direct channel. Monthly cost is twenty dollars for Mailchimp basic, eighty if you go Klaviyo. Twelve-month return is approximately five thousand two hundred dollars in repeat-visit margin and three thousand one hundred dollars in lifted average ticket from segmentation alone. Break-even is month two. The catch: it only works if the direct channel is already converting at a reasonable rate. If your direct channel is dormant, the loyalty layer has nothing to layer onto.
Why the CRM-direct path wins by 2x.

The three competitor models — punch cards, P O S loyalty, standalone loyalty platforms — share a structural problem. They all treat every customer the same. The frequent guest who already comes in every week gets the same 10%-off-after-10-visits offer as the once-a-quarter customer who needs an entirely different intervention. The reward is undifferentiated, so the spend is undifferentiated, so the margin lift is mediocre across the board.

The CRM-direct path lets you segment. A weekly regular gets early access to the chef’s upcoming tasting menu and zero discounts — they don’t need a discount, they need to feel known. A lapsed customer who hasn’t visited in 60 days gets a specific 15 dollars-off-your-next-visit email at day 58 (right before they’d normally lapse to 90+ days). A first-time direct buyer gets a thank-you with their next-time-save offer. Three customers, three different interventions, three different margin profiles. That’s where the 2x comes from.
Why the punch card still beats the standalone platform on R O I.

This is the one that surprises most operators. The punch card returns 750 dollars against 10 dollars in cost — a 75:1 return. The Fivestars/Como standalone returns 2,800 dollars against 2,400 dollars in cost — a 1.17:1 return. The standalone returns more absolute dollars, but the percentage return is worse by a factor of 64. If you have 200 dollars/month to spend on customer marketing, it’s almost never going to be best-spent on the standalone loyalty platform. The same 200 dollars goes further almost anywhere else.

The punch card works because it costs essentially nothing and has a real (if small) behavioral effect on repeat visits. The standalone loyalty platform doesn’t work because its cost structure is too high for the modest behavioral lift it produces. The integrated P O S loyalty sits in between — the cost is low enough that the modest lift still pays back, but only just.
What this means for your setup.

If you have a direct channel that’s already converting: run the CRM-direct path. Klaviyo for the segmentation; your own Stripe/Toast/Square checkout for the order data; a manually-curated regulars list for the highest-value 50 customers; automated re-engagement at day 58. Total monthly cost: 50 dollars–120 dollars depending on email send volume. Total margin lift on a 500-customer base in year one: roughly 5,000 dollars–8,000 dollars in kept margin.

If you don’t have a direct channel: run paper punch cards while you build one. The 750 dollars/year is real money, and the punch card teaches your kitchen staff to track repeat behavior in a way that pays off when you eventually migrate to the CRM-direct path. Don’t spend the 200 dollars/month on a standalone loyalty platform thinking it’s the bridge — it isn’t. It’s a worse-margin version of the punch card with extra complexity.

If you’re already running P O S loyalty: keep it. The break-even is reasonable and the data is real, even if the data is owned by your P O S vendor and gets stranded when you switch processors. Just don’t pay the standalone platform on top of it — that’s a double-spend with overlapping returns.

Don Goldstein manages two DMV restaurants and runs Muntin Digital . The four-model comparison above is from running each variant on the same restaurant between twenty twenty-four and twenty twenty-five.

Key takeaways

Standalone loyalty platforms (Fivestars, Como Sense) cost 165 dollars–249 dollars/month and return ~2,800 dollars/year — a 1.17:1 ratio that loses to the 10 dollars/year punch card on percentage terms.
P O S-integrated loyalty (Toast Rewards, Square Loyalty) sits in the middle on R O I but the data is owned by your processor — it doesn’t come with you if you switch.

The CRM-direct path wins because it lets you segment: weekly regulars get tasting-menu invites with no discount, lapsed customers get a 15 dollars-off email at day 58, first-time direct buyers get a thank-you with a next-visit offer.
Don’t pay both a standalone platform and a P O S-integrated loyalty — that’s a double-spend with overlapping returns.
If your channel mix is wrong (mostly third-party app orders, no direct flow), no loyalty layer fixes it; fix the channel first.
